strengths: Significant dataset contribution addressing real gap: MMEarth-Bench provides 5 global tasks with 12 aligned modalities and explicit geographic test splits, filling a clear need in EO benchmarking that existing work lacks

Comprehensive and honest benchmarking: Evaluates 7 diverse models across multiple seeds with transparent reporting, demonstrating that geographic generalization remains hard (4/5 tasks show substantial performance drops)
Practical model-agnostic method: TTT-MMR consistently improves performance across all models and task types without modifying model architecture, with <1 sec/sample inference cost
Strong scientific practices: Complete reproducibility information, extensive supplementary material with raw results, ablations, and visualizations enabling verification and future work
Clear presentation and commitment to open science: Well-written paper with effective figures, interactive visualization tool, and commitment to release data and code
weaknesses: Limited method novelty: TTT-MMR is a straightforward application of existing joint training and test-time adaptation concepts; per-modality gradient normalization is the only novel technical component and is incremental

Modest and inconsistent improvements: Performance gains from TTT-MMR are often small in absolute terms (Fig. 7), with improvements highly variable across tasks and sometimes starting from negative baselines (soil OC geographic)

Missing comparisons with other TTA methods: No comparison with TENT or other test-time adaptation baselines, making it unclear whether improvements come from test-time training generally or specifically from multimodal aspects

Incomplete analysis of method behavior: Limited ablations (no study of individual modality contribution or gradient normalization impact), unexplained cases where geographic batching underperforms random batching (Table 5), and lack of investigation into what useful adaptation signals emerge during TTT

Unexplored paradox about multimodal inputs: Figure 6 shows multimodal input sometimes hurts geographic generalization, contradicting the paper's motivation, but this critical finding lacks investigation or validation

Fundamental problem not solved: Paper identifies that geographic generalization remains hard for all models but doesn't solve it; TTT-MMR provides partial mitigation rather than addressing underlying causes
Linear probing shows different patterns from finetuning (Fig. S.13) suggesting fine-tuning regime issues, but this is not discussed or investigated
Dataset limited by single-timestamp design (no temporal dynamics), related task types (all environmental monitoring), and lack of analysis regarding spatial representativeness or collection biases

strengths: Addresses genuine gap: Geographic test splits are rare in existing EO benchmarks and are important for evaluating real-world applicability.
Comprehensive experimental design: Evaluation across 7 diverse models, multiple training regimes (5-100% data), proper statistical reporting (3 seeds, error bars).
Well-documented dataset: Detailed procedures for data collection and processing support reproducibility. 12 aligned modalities across all tasks is useful.
Clear empirical findings: Documents significant geographic generalization gaps across all models and shows multimodal inputs can sometimes hurt generalization.
Practical and model-agnostic method: TTT-MMR works across diverse architectures and is computationally efficient (<1 sec/sample).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: TTT-MMR combines existing ideas (joint training with auxiliary losses + test-time adaptation + gradient normalization). Core contribution—using reconstruction losses at test time—is incremental over prior TTA work (TENT, S4T).

Shallow analysis of main finding: Paper identifies geographic generalization gap but provides limited insight into causes. No systematic analysis of distribution shifts, which modalities are affected, or how to fundamentally address the problem.

Modest and inconsistent improvements: Performance gains are small (often ΔR²<0.05), high-variance, and inconsistent across tasks. Method primarily helps weak RGB-only baselines. On soil tasks with negative R² values, improvements are marginal.

Insufficient method validation: No ablations (which components matter?). No comparison with domain adaptation baselines. Weak theoretical justification for why reconstruction loss improves downstream tasks. No analysis of reconstructed modality quality.

Limited task diversity: Only 5 tasks in natural resource monitoring; 4 are regression. Tasks may be solvable with similar spectral features. Some tasks perform very poorly (negative R² on geographic split), raising suitability questions.

Geographic split design concerns: Using Africa as held-out region is somewhat arbitrary. No sensitivity analysis with alternative geographic splits. Potential confounds (Sentinel-2 coverage, cloud conditions, sensor characteristics) not discussed.
Incomplete baselines: Only compared against JT baseline for TTT. No comparison with simpler multimodal fusion approaches or standard domain adaptation methods, limiting insight into method benefits.

Underexplored insights: Linear probing shows smaller geographic gaps than finetuning, suggesting overfitting during encoder tuning, but this is not deeply analyzed. Why include tasks that fail catastrophically (negative R²)?

strengths: Well-designed benchmark addressing real gap: first with 12 aligned modalities across all tasks and explicit geographic test splits for systematic evaluation of out-of-distribution generalization
Comprehensive evaluation: 7 diverse models, 3 data regimes, 3 random seeds, both finetuning and linear probing across in-distribution and geographic splits
Important findings: documents substantial geographic generalization gap (4 of 5 tasks) and counterintuitive result that multimodal finetuning can hurt geographic robustness
High-quality dataset curation: careful source selection, filtering procedures, global coverage with balanced sampling, detailed documentation enabling reproduction

Model-agnostic method with consistent improvements: TTT-MMR works across all architectures without modifications; per-modality gradient normalization and geographic batching provide good specialization/regularization tradeoff
Strong reproducibility: raw results tables, detailed supplementary procedures, promised code/data release, interactive visualization tool
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is incremental: TTT-MMR combines existing ideas (joint training, test-time training, multimodal reconstruction); per-modality gradient normalization is the main novel component but limited in scope

Modest performance improvements: typical gains of 0.01-0.08 on random split, near-zero on geographic split for biomass; while statistically significant, practical improvements are limited and don't solve identified geographic generalization problem

Geographic test split design limited to single region (Africa): conclusions about geographic generalization rest on one geographic shift; would be substantially stronger with 2-3 held-out regions; Africa selection somewhat arbitrary despite reasonable motivation

Key findings underdeveloped: multimodal-input-hurts-generalization result (Fig. 6) lacks deep investigation—unclear if phenomenon is architecture/modality/task-specific or how to address it beyond TTT-MMR

Missing comparative analysis: no comparison to other TTT methods, limited engagement with domain adaptation literature, no per-modality ablations to understand contribution to geographic generalization

Practical applicability gaps: unclear if 12 modalities available at inference time; data completeness varies by task (Fig. S.2); climate data limited (only 3 modalities); no discussion of computational cost/benefit
Evaluation metric limitations: R² can be misleading when negative or near-zero (common for soil tasks); limits interpretation of improvement magnitude
Task diversity limited: species task restricted to 100 mammals with tile-level labels; no other taxa; soil tasks could benefit from richer climate data

strengths: Well-designed multimodal benchmark addressing real gaps: 12 aligned modalities, global distribution, random + geographic test splits, multiple training regimes (5%, 50%, 100%)
Large-scale dataset: ~77K tiles across 5 novel environmental tasks with careful curation from authoritative sources (GEDI, WoSIS, IUCN)

Comprehensive benchmarking of 8 diverse pretrained models revealing important insights: geographic generalization remains poor, pretraining benefits diminish with sufficient data, randomly initialized multimodal models are competitive
Strong experimental rigor: three random seeds, detailed hyperparameters, extensive raw results, clear reproducibility plan
TTT-MMR is model-agnostic, works with any architecture/loss, demonstrates practical improvements especially on long-tail distributions with geographic batching
Geographic test split thoughtfully targets underrepresented regions (Africa) in labeled EO data, addressing real societal bias
Interactive visualization tool and commitment to code/data release enhance community value
weaknesses: Geographic generalization testing limited to single continent (Africa only)—claims of 'global' evaluation undermined by lack of multiple held-out regions
TTT-MMR method lacks novelty: straightforward application of existing TTA to multimodal setting without comparison to other TTA baselines (TENT, etc.); improvements modest (~0.01-0.03 R²)
Insufficient mechanistic analysis of why geographic generalization fails despite global pretraining—no investigation of representation shifts, error distributions, or specific domain shift sources
Critical information scattered across appendix: linear probing results, modality importance analysis, architectural details—weakens main narrative
Dataset design limitations: all tasks continuous (no diverse classification), single timestamp (no temporal dynamics), fixed 10m resolution, no discussion of label noise for remotely sensed proxies

Missing ablations: no systematic evaluation of different fusion strategies for multimodal models, no analysis of modality dropout during finetuning, limited modality importance analysis (one model/seed)

Method evaluation gaps: no comparison to simpler domain adaptation baselines, no convergence analysis for TTT iterations, statistical testing insufficient (overlapping error bars, limited significance tests)
Experimental design choices underexplored: parameter-efficient fine-tuning (adapters, LoRA) not compared, finetuning vs. linear probing insights relegated to appendix

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing a genuine gap in Earth observation: 5 environmental tasks with 12 aligned modalities across all tasks, significantly more than existing benchmarks (2-4 modalities)
Comprehensive dataset design with explicit geographic test splits using Africa as underrepresented region, plus multiple training data regimes (5%, 50%, 100%) enabling low-shot evaluation
Thorough benchmarking of 8 diverse pretrained models spanning multiple architectures (ConvNet, ViT, Swin) with both unimodal and multimodal variants
Strong empirical findings: systematic demonstration that geographic generalization is severely limited despite global pretraining, which is important for the community to understand
TTT-MMR is model-agnostic and shows consistent improvements across all 8 models and both test splits; geographic batching provides meaningful regularization-specialization trade-off
Excellent reproducibility emphasis with extensive appendix documentation, implementation details, hyperparameters, and promised code/dataset release
Practical method that could benefit practitioners working with multimodal Earth observation data in limited-label settings
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core method: TTT-MMR applies existing test-time training concepts (Sun et al. 2020; Gandelsman et al. 2022) with straightforward per-modality gradient normalization; no comparison with TENT, READ, or other TTA baselines to establish necessity

Modest empirical improvements often near practical significance thresholds: ~0.01 R² on biomass, near-zero or negative for soil OC geographic split, sometimes worsening performance for specific models (Table A.15, negative RI for Galileo/ConvNeXtV2A-MM)

Insufficient analysis of why TTT-MMR works: limited investigation of which modalities drive improvements (Fig. A.16 shown only for one model/seed/split), no architecture-specific analysis, missing ablation studies on hyperparameters (λ, batch size, I_max), no exploration of alternative normalization schemes

Core geographic generalization challenge remains largely unsolved: all models perform very poorly on Africa (soil OC R² often <-1.0), TTT-MMR provides only modest relief, and paper lacks explanation of why global pretraining fails to help
Potential test-set leakage: using validation set to select I_max based on test-set structure (page 9); while indirect, information about test-set characteristics informs hyperparameter selection
Missing ablation studies on critical design choices: hyperparameters appear hand-tuned (batch size 8, λ=10⁻², I_max=5) with no sensitivity analysis; geographic batching parameters untested

Dataset limitations not deeply explored: single-timestamp design may limit ecological realism, no analysis of distribution shifts within regions, species task limited to terrestrial mammals (incomplete taxonomic coverage), arbitrary geographic test region choice not fully justified

Insufficient experimental comparisons: no ablation between JT+TTT vs. JT+standard finetuning on test data, no comparison with test-time augmentation baselines, missing comparison with domain adaptation methods (UDA-SS, adapters)
Insufficient analysis of key counterintuitive findings: multimodal input hurts geographic generalization for some tasks (Fig. 6)—finding deserves but lacks deep investigation and explanation
Presentation issues: 64-page manuscript is overly dense, key results relegated to appendix, method section could be more concise, figure fonts often unreadable, dataset/code links appear redacted

strengths: Novel and well-designed benchmark addressing genuine gap: 12 aligned modalities, global distribution, and explicit geographic test splits (Africa held-out) differentiate from existing EO benchmarks which typically have 1-3 modalities and limited geographic evaluation

Exceptional dataset curation with five diverse environmental tasks (biomass, soil properties, species occurrence), thoughtful modality selection spanning pixel-level sensors and tile-level climate variables, and rigorous geographic stratification

Comprehensive and rigorous benchmarking of 8 pretrained models across diverse architectures and pretraining approaches, with multiple evaluation regimes (finetuning, linear probing, 5%/50%/100% training data)

Important empirical findings clearly demonstrated: persistent geographic generalization gap despite global pretraining, competitive performance of randomly-initialized multimodal models with sufficient labeled data, and clear evidence of modality mismatch problem

Practical and model-agnostic TTT-MMR method with consistent improvements across all models/tasks/splits; geographic batching introduces interpretable regularization-specialization trade-off; particularly beneficial for long-tail distributions
Exceptional reproducibility: comprehensive appendix with implementation details, clear data format (H5 files), Python code examples, multiple random seeds throughout, and promised code/data release

Well-executed experimental design with both random and geographic test splits enabling rigorous distribution shift analysis, long-tail performance analysis revealing differential effects, and statistical significance testing
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in TTT-MMR: test-time training and reconstruction-based auxiliary tasks are established techniques; main contribution is application to multimodal EO rather than fundamental algorithmic advance; lacks theoretical justification for why this specific approach helps

Incomplete analysis of geographic generalization gap: while demonstrated clearly, the paper analyzes why insufficiently—missing feature-level analysis of which modalities transfer, domain shift characterization (optical properties, sensor differences, seasonal variations), and investigation of failure modes for poorly-generalizing models

TTT-MMR evaluation concerns: modest improvements on random split (0.01-0.05 R²); validation set usage to select iteration count raises potential data leakage questions; modality ablation shown for single seed only; missing experimental comparison to other TTA methods (TENT mentioned but not compared)

Unexplained empirical phenomena reducing confidence: randomly-initialized ConvNeXtV2A-MM outperforms some pretrained models on random split; Figure 6 shows multimodal finetuning sometimes hurts geographic generalization; variable model ranking across tasks with no clear pattern explained

Hyperparameter choices underexplored: batch size (8), learning rate (10⁻²), iteration count (5) selected without sensitivity analysis; geographic batching strategy appears task-specific with unclear generalization; no comparison of alternative gradient normalization strategies

Benchmark design questions: imbalanced task types (4 regression, 1 classification); spatial scale concerns (128×128 = ~1.6 km² receptive field); modality relevance varies by task but not systematically explored; species task multi-label distribution with imbalanced classes

Limited scope of generalization discussion: method and insights are Earth observation-specific with unclear applicability to other multimodal domains (robotics, medical imaging); geographic generalization findings may not inform broader multimodal ML community

Presentation density and organization: 64-page document with important results relegated to appendix; Figure 8 (long-tail analysis) difficult to parse; method formulation could be more concise; linear probing results show different patterns than finetuning but receive minimal discussion
